docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This course will explore ability, disability, and accessibility. It introduces students to the theory, history, policy, and practice of accessibility and inclusion in computing. Course readings will explore relevant concepts from disability studies, accessibility, human-computer interaction, and design methods. Most accessibility content focuses on web accessibility for people who are blind or low-vision. In addition, through this course, you will learn how to design for people with different abilities including hearing loss, motor impairments, cognitive decline, and neurodiversity. As early adopters, people with disabilities have inspired a host of future user interface technologies, e.g., conversational assistants, text-to-speech, speech recognition, optical character recognition, predictive typing, tactile displays, etc. People with disabilities continue to be the first users of interface next-generation technologies that are gradually adopted widely. We will discuss how to design online and offline; how to design for visible and invisible disabilities; and how to design for permanent, situational, and temporary disabilities.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
This course will explore ability, disability, and accessibility. It introduces students to the theory, history, policy, and practice of accessibility and inclusion in computing. Course readings will explore relevant concepts from disability studies, accessibility, human-computer interaction, and design methods. Through this course, you will learn how to design for people with different abilities including blind or low vision, hearing loss, motor impairments, cognitive decline, and neurodiversity. As early adopters, people with disabilities have inspired a host of future user interface technologies, e.g., conversational assistants, text-to-speech, speech recognition, optical character recognition, predictive typing, tactile displays, etc. People with disabilities continue to be the first users of next-generation interface technologies that are gradually adopted more widely including Gen-AI and image recognition tools. We will discuss how to design online and offline; how to design for visible and invisible disabilities; and how to design for permanent, situational, and temporary disabilities.

Students will leave the course with a sense of:

  • What access technologies already exist and what technologies are emerging
  • Critique different models of disability based on literature in disability studies
  • Define and distinguish between web accessibility guidelines and legislation
  • What it takes to both create and use accessible computing systems for people with visible and invisible disabilities
  • How to make interfaces and interactions more accessible
  • How to make documents accessible and conduct inclusive presentations and meetings
  • Critically discuss accessibility approaches of different media formats across disabilities

docs.title: Pre-Requisites
docs.text: There are no prerequisites for this course. However, some prior programming experience or knowledge of web programming is helpful but not required.

docs.title: Project Context
docs.text: Everyone has various senses and abilities, many of whom do not match your own. When creating slide presentations or documents, it is important to consider how to make them accessible to everyone. In this assignment, you will learn to use Adobe Acrobat to modify PDF documents to be accessible and follow guidelines to make more accessible presentation slide decks.

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
This is an individual assignment. There are two (2) parts for this homework. Your final submission on Canvas will be one PDF file.

A) Create an Accessible PDF - 25 points

B) Create an Accessible Presentation - 50 points

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: The goal of this assignment is to create an accessible PDF from an inaccessible one. We will list instructions here, but they are pulled from a larger document helpfully put together for the CHI 2021 conference.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: Download the assignment file and open using Adobe Acrobat Pro

docs.title: Using the tools at the left side of the application find the Prepare for Accessibility Tool
docs.text:
1. Run the Check for Accessibility Tool. This tool will generate an accessibility report which you will turn in along with your accessibile PDF document (Make note of where this report is saved so you can find it later). In Acrobat this should open up a pane on the right side showing several issues with the current document including:
  2. Document Issues
    • Tagged PDF
    • Logical Reading Order
    • Primary Language
    • Color Contrast
  3. Page Content
    • Document Tags
    • Tab Order
  4. Alternate Text
    • Figures have no Alternative Text
  5. Tables
    • Table Content not properly tagged
    • Rows
    • TH and TD
    • Headers
    • Regularity
  6. Lists
    • Not Properly Tagged
  7. Headings
    • Not Properly Nested

docs.title: Fix Accessibility Issues
docs.text:
1. Add Accessibility Tags to the document
  2. Using the Prepare for Accessibilty Tool > Automatically tag PDF
  3. Fix Tab Order
  4. Open Thumbnail View for the PDF pages using the toolbar on the right
  5. Select all pages
  6. Right Click and select page properties
  7. Select Use Document Structure
  8. Update the metadata by going to File > Document Properties
  9. Set Author Name: On the Description tab set the author name to "YOUR NAME - Andrew ID"
  10. Set Primary Language: On the Advanced tab, under Reading Options set the langauge.
  11. Check for Logical Reading Order
  12. Under the Prepare for Accessibility tool, Open the Fix Reading Order panel.
  13. The document should now show highlighted and numbered sections. These sections should be properly separated and numbered according to the logical order they should be read on the page. NOTE: Make sure the Page Content Groups > Page Content Order Options are selected.
  14. Fix Improperly Tagged Elements using the Reading Order tool
  15. Highlight the content you want to tag then click the proper tag using the reading order tool. You can use this guidance on using the tool if you get stuck. Be sure to pay attention to:
    1. Headings vs Content
      1. Tables vs Figures
  16. Add Alternative Text for Figures
  17. Using the Prepare for Accessibility Tool (Left Side), click Add alternate text
  18. Add text descriptions for each instructor and teaching assistant image.
  19. Run the Check for Accessibility tool again to make sure you've addressed all issues.
  20. Save the PDF again, close it, and reopen it to double-check that your accessibility features have been saved.
  21. Turn in the Final PDF .

docs.text: Submit the final PDF to Canvas.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Many presentation tools, like Powerpoint and Google Slides, have Accessibility Checker functions. While these tools are helpful, they can not catch all the problems that pop up in presentations. For this, we offer a checklist that you can use to consider various aspects of slide and presentation design that can improve its accessibility to a variety of audiences.

ASSETS is the premier conference in ACM SIGCHI for presenting work related to accessibility for people with disabilities. The conference organizers have developed this handy presentation guide for conference talk authors to ensure that their entire audience can understand your talk. We include some of their guidelines below in the homework assignment. Hopefully (fingers crossed!) they don't conflict too much.

Some other guides include:

  1. University of Washington Professor Richard Ladner's paper, "Making Your Conference Talk Accessible."
  2. Kyle Rector's video on accessible presentations.
  3. W3C guide on preparing slides and projected material.
  4. Microsoft's web guide to making accessible PowerPoint presentations.
  5. Microsoft's video guide to making accessible PowerPoint presentations.
  6. University of Washington DO-IT Center's guide to presenting accessibly.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Choose one of the following presentations to make more accessible.

  1. Bad Presentation
  2. Chicken Chicken
  3. Design a Presentation
  4. Dolphins
  5. How to Give a Great Seminar
  6. Malaria
  7. Synergy
  8. Verbal Communication

Warning

These presentations have been sourced on the Internet. Some are short, some are long. Some contain technical content; some appear to be jokes. Whichever one you pick, as you edit them for accessibility, be careful to preserve your understanding of the authors' original intent. Whenever possible, do not change their message.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Run through the following checklist and fix any issues that you see in the presentation.

    1. Slides
      1. My slides have slide numbers.
      2. I minimized the number of slides down to the essential ones for explaining my message.
      3. I removed unnecessary distractions in the slide content (minimal in design).
      4. My slides have text on them that is readable by text-to-speech software (rather than text embedded as bitmap pictures).
      5. My talk shows an indication of progress as I move through it.
      6. I display information progressively (e.g., sequential highlighting).
      7. My slides highlight and emphasize key elements in text, graphics, and formulas.
    2. Graphics
      1. My graphics have alternate text descriptions. (Google Slides, Microsoft Office).
      2. I use high contrast colors (> 4:1) for background/foreground.
      3. I use color-blind friendly color palettes (Make a palette).
      4. I minimize my use of animations.
      5. I ensure there is sufficient space between graphical items.
      6. I minimize the number of visuals on each slide.
      7. I use effective graphics with minimal design flourishes.
      8. I provide secondary notation by using visual analogues to represent emphasis and prosody (e.g., emoticons, symbols, or images).
      9. I provided visual analogues (e.g. diagrams, charts, notations) for any music/ sound.
    3. Embedded Videos
      1. I added closed captioning to every embedded video.
      2. I provided written transcripts for every embedded video and audio clips.
      3. I added audio descriptions (e.g. described video) for every embedded video. Optional for HW1
      4. I used appropriate punctuation enabling screen readers and text-to-speech engines to work well.
      5. I embedded definitions for vocabulary and symbols within the text (e.g., via hyperlinks or footnotes).
      6. I followed accessibility standards (NIMAS, DAISY) when creating digital text.
    4. Text
      1. I used large fonts (> 18 pt).
      2. I minimized the amount of text in each slide.
      3. I avoided using complex words when simpler ones would do.
      4. I ensured there is sufficient space between lines of text.
      5. I provided visual and/or emotional descriptions to help interpret music/sound.
      6. I embedded visual, non-linguistic support for vocabulary clarification (pictures, videos, etc.)
    5. Recorded Audio
      1. I spoke every word that appears on the slide.
      2. I spoke loudly and clearly.
      3. I used terminology understandable to non-native speakers (e.g. avoid slang).
      4. I spoke at a moderate pace (around 100-150 words per minute).
      5. I provided a voice narration for embedded math equations (Math ML)
    6. Recorded Presentation
      1. I verbally described all important images and charts.
      2. I verbally described all animations.
      3. I paused between slides.
      4. If I skipped a slide or an element on a slide, I said so out loud.
      5. I referred to the slide numbers in my presentation.
      6. To enable lip reading, I faced the audience (i.e. camera) and adjusted it to ensure my lips are clearly visible.
      7. I minimized my use of the mouse pointer.
      8. Whenever I used the mouse pointer in my talk, I described the action verbally.

  2. Record yourself making the presentation.

    1. Open the slides in the latest desktop version of Microsoft PowerPoint.
    2. Choose the Record menu.
    3. If you feel comfortable doing so, choose the Cameo option to insert a recording of you narrating the slides on the lower right hand corner of the slide deck.
    4. Choose the Record button in the top right of the PowerPoint UI.
    5. Once you have finished recording, choose File/Export... from the menu and export your video as an MP4.
    6. Upload the video to YouTube; please make sure it's set to private.

docs.title: Submission
docs.text:
There are two items to submit for this homework part. Add a page to your accessible PDF that includes the links to these two items.

  1. Presentation
    1. Copy the slide deck into your Google Drive.
    2. Open the file in Google Slides.
    3. Choose File/Share/Sharing with Others from the menu.
    4. Change the Sharing permissions from General Access Restricted to General Access Carnegie Mellon University.
    5. Press the Copy link button and submit that link to canvas.
  2. Recorded Narration
    1. Submit the private link to your uploaded YouTube video to canvas.
